{{nihongo|'''Junichiro Itani'''|伊谷 純一郎|Itani Jun'ichirō|May 9, 1926 &ndash; August 19, 2001}} was a Japanese [[anthropologist]] who served as a professor [[emeritus]] at [[Kyoto University]] and as president of the Primate Society of Japan. He is considered a founder of the discipline of Japanese [[primatology]].

==Biography==
Junichiro Itani was born at [[Tottori (city)|Tottori]]. His father, Kenzo Itani, was a [[Yōga]] painter. 

He entered [[Kyoto University]], [[Graduate School of Science and Faculty of Science, Kyoto University|Faculty of Science]]. He majored in [[ethology]] under [[Kinji Imanishi]], eventually becoming one of the leading figures in Japanese primatology.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Asquith |first=Pamela |title=Naked Science: Anthropological Inquiry Into Boundaries, Power, and Knowledge |publisher=Routledge |year=1996 |editor-last=Nader |editor-first=Laura |location=New York & London |publication-date=1996 |pages=249 |chapter=Japanese Science and Western Hegemonies: Primatology and the Limits Set to Questions}}</ref> He received a [[Bachelor of Science|BS]] in March 1951, and became a researcher at [[Japan Monkey Centre]], [[Inuyama, Aichi]]. He observed [[Japanese macaque|Japanese macaques]] at [[Takasakiyama Natural Zoological Garden]].<ref>''[[The Nikkei]]'': [https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXLASJB13H1Y_T10C16A4960E00/ (2016.4.22)]</ref> In 1962, he submitted his doctoral dissertation titled ''"Communication of wild Japanese macaque"(野生ニホンザルのコミュニケーションに関する研究)''.<ref>[https://ci.nii.ac.jp/naid/500000317400 CiNii (dissertation)]</ref> 

He became an assistant professor at [[Kyoto University]], Faculty of Science in October 1962, and was promoted to professor in 1981. He founded the [[Primate Research Institute]] and the Center for African Area Studies at that university in 1986, and he served as the first chief of the latter center until his retirement.<ref>[https://www.africa.kyoto-u.ac.jp/archives/members/emeritus_itani CAAS]</ref> He retired from Kyoto University in 1990 and became a professor at [[Kobe Gakuin University]] (until 1998). 

He died at age 75 of [[pneumonia]].

As with most Japanese primatologists, his early research was on [[Japanese macaque]]s ''(Macaca fuscata)'', but most of his career focused on African primates, especially [[chimpanzee]]s (''Pan troglodytes''). He started research in Africa in 1958. The majority of his work was based around the social structures of primate society.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2001/08/21/national/obituaries-junichiro-itani-sumiko-takahara/|title = Obituaries: Junichiro Itani, Sumiko Takahara|date = 21 August 2001}}</ref>

==Awards==
*[[Asahi Prize]] (1968)
*The [[Thomas Henry Huxley|Huxley]] Award in Anthropology ([[Royal Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland|Royal Anthropological Institute]], [[London]]. (1984)
*[[Medals of Honor (Japan)]](Medal with Purple Ribbon) (1992)
*[[Order of the Sacred Treasure]]

==Books available in English==
* ''Japanese Monkeys in Takasakiyama'' (1954)
* ''Hominid culture in primate perspective'' / Duane Quiatt and Junichiro Itani, editors (1994)
* ''A Comparative study of ecological anthropology in tropical Africa ''
* ''Great Ape Societies'' by [[William McGrew|William C McGrew]]; [[Linda Marchant|Linda F Marchant]]; [[Toshisada Nishida]]; [[Jane Goodall]] and Junichiro Itani

==Relatives==
*Father: Kenzo Itani(伊谷賢蔵) was a [[Yōga]] painter. He studied at [[Kyoto Institute of Technology|Higher Technical School, Kyoto]]. He learned [[Yōga]] under [[Jutaro Kuroda]]. He lived as a painter and taught painting at [[Kyoto University of Education]].
*Son: Genichi Itani (伊谷原一) is an [[anthropologist]] ([[primatology]]). He worked at [[Primate Research Institute]]
*Son: Juichi Itani (伊谷樹一) is an [[agriculturist]].
